title: JavaScript event loop
core: The call stack holds the frames of the functions that run now
The task queue holds callbacks that wait for the stack to empty
The event loop moves one task to the stack when the stack is empty
Microtasks run after the current task and before the next task
A long task blocks rendering and input until it ends

questions.prompt: What does the JavaScript **call stack** hold?
questions.answer: The frames of the functions that are running now

obviousWrong.text: The CSS rules that the browser applies to the page
obviousWrong.rationale: CSS rules live in the CSSOM, not in the call stack.

plausibleWrong.text: The callbacks that wait for the next event loop turn
plausibleWrong.rationale: Waiting callbacks live in a task queue until the stack is empty.

plausibleWrong.text: The objects that the garbage collector can free
plausibleWrong.rationale: Objects live in the heap. The stack holds frames.

questions.explanation: Each function call pushes a frame. The frame leaves the stack when the function returns.

questions.prompt: Where does a callback from `setTimeout` wait before it runs?

obviousWrong.rationale: The address bar shows the URL. It does not hold callbacks.

plausibleWrong.rationale: Promise reactions use the microtask queue. Timers use the task queue.

plausibleWrong.text: On the call stack, below the current frame
plausibleWrong.rationale: A timer callback is not on the stack until the event loop picks it.

questions.explanation: The timer adds a task to the task queue when the delay ends.

questions.prompt: When does the event loop run the microtasks?
questions.answer: After the current task ends, before the next task starts

obviousWrong.text: Only when the user reloads the page
obviousWrong.rationale: A reload starts a new page. Microtasks run on each turn.

plausibleWrong.text: After all tasks in the task queue are done
plausibleWrong.rationale: Microtasks do not wait for the task queue to empty.

plausibleWrong.text: At the same time as the current task, on a second thread
plausibleWrong.rationale: The event loop runs on one thread. Microtasks do not run in parallel.

questions.explanation: The loop empties the microtask queue after each task.

questions.prompt: Which statement about `await` in an `async` function is true?
questions.answer: It pauses the function and resumes it in a microtask

obviousWrong.text: It deletes the function from memory
obviousWrong.rationale: The function keeps its state while it waits.

plausibleWrong.text: It blocks the thread until the promise settles
plausibleWrong.rationale: Other code can run while the function waits.

plausibleWrong.text: It resumes the function in a new task from the task queue
plausibleWrong.rationale: The continuation is a microtask, not a task.

questions.explanation: The function yields at `await`. A promise reaction resumes it.

obviousWrong.text: Nothing, because the code has a syntax error

plausibleWrong.rationale: The promise reaction is a microtask, so it runs before the timer task.
A delay of 0 still queues a task. The synchronous log runs first.

questions.explanation: Synchronous code runs first. Then the microtask runs. The timer task runs last.

questions.prompt: A microtask queues a new microtask each time it runs. What occurs?
questions.answer: The page stops rendering and stops handling events

obviousWrong.text: The browser closes the tab to protect the user
obviousWrong.rationale: The browser does not close the tab for this.

plausibleWrong.text: The event loop runs one task between each microtask
plausibleWrong.rationale: The loop empties the microtask queue before it runs a task.

plausibleWrong.text: The engine moves the extra microtasks to the task queue
plausibleWrong.rationale: The engine does not move microtasks between queues.

questions.explanation: The microtask queue never becomes empty, so the loop never reaches rendering or tasks.

questions.prompt: Why can a long loop of `await` calls on promises that are already resolved still freeze the page?
questions.answer: Each resume is a microtask, so no task or render can run between them

obviousWrong.text: Because `await` sends a network request each time

plausibleWrong.text: Because each `await` creates a new thread that competes for the CPU
plausibleWrong.rationale: JavaScript on the page runs on one thread.

plausibleWrong.text: Because resolved promises go to the task queue in a random order
plausibleWrong.rationale: Reactions use the microtask queue in a fixed order.

questions.explanation: The chain stays in the microtask queue until it ends, so rendering waits.

questions.prompt: You must process 1 million items without a frozen page. Which design is correct?
questions.answer: Process a batch, then schedule the next batch as a new task

obviousWrong.text: Delete the items that the page does not show
obviousWrong.rationale: Deleting data does not do the work that the task requires.

plausibleWrong.text: Process each item in its own `Promise.resolve().then()` callback
plausibleWrong.rationale: All the callbacks are microtasks, so rendering still waits for all of them.

plausibleWrong.text: Wrap the loop in an `async` function with no `await`
plausibleWrong.rationale: An `async` function with no `await` runs to the end in one go.

questions.explanation: A new task lets the browser render and handle events between batches.
